sources.title: National Park Service: Shoshone, adapted expedition journals of 1805
sources.note: Uses only attributed August 1805 observations. NPS explicitly modernizes and excerpts the journals; no verbatim historic quotations used. Introductory contemporary location and reservation-dissolution claims are erroneous or confusing and are excluded.

sources.title: Yellowstone National Park: Earliest Humans
sources.note: Increased Use section associates Intermountain Ware with Shoshone roughly 700 years ago; earlier archaeology is not assigned wholesale to a living nation.

sources.title: Eastern Shoshone Tribe: About
sources.note: Selected Washakie, 1863 and 1868 treaty and Wind River history. Contested Sacagawea death location, absolute first-horse claim and very early archaeological ethnicity omitted.

sources.title: Utah State Archives: Mae Timbimboo Parry, Stories of Utah Women
sources.note: Maren Peterson, December 8, 2020; high-school oral-history work and historical terminology. Casualty estimates and biographical school classifications not used.

sources.title: National Park Service: The Timbisha Shoshone Demonstration Project
sources.note: Nicole Martin; houses, shared water tap, destruction and community-led land campaign. Avoid conflicting house counts in different NPS publications.

sources.title: University of Utah Shoshoni Language Project: Dictionary, H entries
sources.note: Exact Hakanni e? / How are you? entry, marked Duck Valley, Crum, Crum, and Dayley 2002. Direct table and indexed original checked; quote retains original spelling.

sources.title: University of Utah: Shoshoni Talking Dictionary
sources.note: Archived project history: Ely collaboration beginning 2008; youth apprenticeship and later community recordings. No assertion that archived program currently runs.

sources.title: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes: Language and Culture
sources.note: Official public description of archives, land claims, family histories and separate language instruction. Does not treat Bannock and Shoshone as one language.

sources.title: Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation: History
sources.note: Arikara/Sahnish section; sacred migration account, distinct language and repeated movements. Uses early 1860s for Star Village/Like-a-Fishhook transition because exact years differ across institutional accounts.

sources.title: Mary Jane Schneider: Arikaras, Encyclopedia of the Great Plains
sources.note: University of North Dakota author, University of Nebraska-Lincoln publication; gardening, seasonal movements, family housing, pottery and baskets.

sources.title: North Dakota Studies: Section 1, Arikaras
sources.note: Original institutional indexed full text checked using site.ndstudies.gov/gr8/node/554 "beds"; direct fetch failed. Lodge layout and dried meat selected; nutritional oil assertions and photo-site location omitted.

sources.title: Kansas Historical Society: Arikara
sources.note: Trade in surplus produce with other Plains peoples. No population estimates adopted.

sources.title: North Dakota Studies: Section 2, Farming
sources.note: Image 6 explicitly identifies Arikara women retaining family gardens while men farmed and ranched. Does not assign Hidatsa Maxidiwiac, generic Fort Berthold antler-rake photographs or Mandan James Holding Eagle to Arikara ethnicity.

sources.title: Wendi Field Murray: Getting to Know Star Village
sources.note: State Historical Society of North Dakota, July 25, 2016; 1908 Stout notes, Bull Neck interview via Alex Sage, 22 of 94 lodge residents, structures 26, 30 and 32.

sources.title: Jo Lea Wetherilt Behrens: Arikara War, Encyclopedia of the Great Plains
sources.note: University of Nebraska at Omaha author; 1823 trade conflict, expedition and Pilcher burning villages after military departure.

sources.title: State Historical Society of North Dakota: Fort Clark History
sources.note: 1837 smallpox and Arikara occupation of abandoned Mandan village in 1838; avoid unsafely precise mortality figures.

sources.title: Marcus Wells Jr.: Senate Indian Affairs Committee testimony, November 15, 2007
sources.note: PDF title page identifies Marcus Wells Jr., despite erroneous extraction metadata title. Printed pp. 3, 5 and 10: bottomland losses, 1953 closure and 1954 completion, relocation and water hauling. No unsupported medical causation adopted.

sources.title: MHA Nation: Language
sources.note: Official Arikara language section prints Thank you! followed by wetAxkoosšteéRAt!; exact mixed-case spelling retained. Online lesson archives and materials also directly visible.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One broad card only; no automatic association with eastern-shoshone, lemhi-shoshone or newe-western-shoshone.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: Index 1530 to 1783; decoded world-1530 feature bbox [-118.0326,35.7803,-105.1157,45.5307]. Great Basin and Rocky Mountain coverage spans multiple communities. Public opening explains collective identity and coverage dates.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: Timbisha example explicitly identified as a southern regional community. Early outline cannot establish exact boundaries or one shared government. Journal wrapper has erroneous Lemhi/Wind River and reservation-dissolution statements, excluded; only attributed 1805 observations used.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Distinct Arikara/Sahnish narrative only; no composite MHA or Mandan/Hidatsa association.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: Index 1530 to 1783; decoded world-1530 feature bbox [-101.2708,44.7151,-99.9784,46.3544], Missouri corridor in South/North Dakota. This is one phase of shifting village geography, not full migration territory.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: Institutional histories variously date Star Village/Like-a-Fishhook transition 1861, 1862 or 1863; public prose uses early 1860s and periods are broad. Fort Clark 1838 occupation follows a Mandan village, not its original founding. Garrison displacement totals explicitly cover all three affiliated tribes. Maxidiwiac is Hidatsa and not used as an Arikara example. No precontact alphabet claimed.
